content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice blend is a 100% natural juice made from a mix of citrus fruits (orange, mandarin, grapefruit, lemon). The juice contains no added sugar, preservatives or colourings. It offers a bright aroma, refreshing taste and a high vitamin C content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is produced from carefully selected fruits grown without pesticides.
Citrus fruits are rich in flavonoids that help protect blood vessels.
In 2022 the product received an “Organic” certification for meeting ecological standards.
The juice is packaged in dark‑glass bottles that protect vitamin C from light degradation.
Each 250 ml bottle provides more than 70 % of the adult daily recommended intake of vitamin C.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, supports collagen synthesis and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: The juice is almost entirely water, helping to maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 ml of juice contains about 45 kcal, making it suitable for diet‑friendly nutrition.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in citrus help combat free radicals.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to citrus fruits.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Large doses of vitamin C may affect the efficacy of certain medications, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: The juice is best served chilled, optionally diluted with water. It can be used in smoothies, cocktails, marinades, and as a base for fruit desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in the refrigerator at 2 °C–8 °C. Once opened, consume within 5 days. Do not freeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Gordita is a traditional Mexican corn‑maize flatbread made from masa (corn dough) and filled with a savory stuffing. This version uses seasoned beans (3345) as the filling, giving the dish a hearty flavor and an extra boost of plant protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gorditas are commonly eaten for breakfast, lunch or dinner and are designed to be handheld.
Beans are considered a “food of the gods” in Mexican cuisine and appear in countless dishes.
The dough for gorditas is leaven‑free, resulting in a soft yet slightly chewy texture.
Traditionally they are cooked on a hot griddle or open flame, which creates a lightly toasted crust.
The bean‑filled version is popular among vegetarians for its protein content.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The combination of corn masa and beans leads to a slower rise in blood sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beans are a good source of folate and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking beans before cooking helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Sodium in prepared filling
items.content: If the bean filling is salted, monitor overall sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the gordita hot, split it open and top with fresh vegetables, salsa, guacamole or sour cream. It works well as a snack or as part of a complete meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared gorditas in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in an oven or on a skillet before serving.

stewed-seasoned-ground-beef-and-pork-mex.title: Stewed, seasoned, ground beef and pork, Mexican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed, seasoned, ground beef and pork, Mexican style (1270) is a ready‑to‑eat meat blend made from beef and pork, flavored with traditional Mexican spices and slowly stewed until tender. It is convenient for tacos, burritos, chili, pie fillings and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mexican seasoning typically includes chili, cumin, oregano, paprika and garlic, giving the blend its characteristic aroma.
The beef‑pork combination balances flavor: beef adds depth, pork adds juiciness.
Low‑heat stewing preserves most nutrients and makes the meat easy to digest.
The product is widely used in fast‑food outlets and cafeterias where quick preparation without flavor loss is essential.
Traditional Mexican ground meat often contains a touch of tomato paste to enhance taste.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The beef‑pork blend provides a rich source of complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is abundant in vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Pork contributes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that are important for heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Chili and cumin contain antioxidant compounds that may help reduce inflammation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Seasonings can add salt; people monitoring sodium intake should account for this in their overall diet.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Pork adds saturated fat; moderate consumption is advised for those with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to chili, coriander or other spices used in the blend.

items.title: Requires thorough cooking
items.content: To eliminate pathogenic bacteria, the meat should be heated to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C (160 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready for use after reheating. Add it to tacos, burritos, chili, soups, casseroles, or use as a filling for peppers or tortillas. For extra brightness, top with fresh cilantro, lime juice and avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0–4 °C in the original packaging for up to 5 days after opening. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

taco-corn-tortilla-with-beans-cheese.title: Corn Tortilla with Beans and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A corn tortilla filled with black beans and shredded cheese is a classic Mexican taco. The tortilla is soft and slightly sweet, while the filling is hearty, flavorful, and nutritious.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn tortillas have been used in Mexico for over 3,000 years.
Black beans are rich in antioxidants and are considered a superfood in Latin American cuisine.
Traditional Mexican cheese such as queso fresco has a mild, slightly tangy flavor and a crumbly texture.
Tacos are traditionally folded in half and served with salsa, guacamole, or a squeeze of lime.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans and cheese together provide a complete set of amino acids that support muscle repair and tissue maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Black beans contain both soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Beans and corn flour are good sources of thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, nutrients important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Corn tortillas have a lower glycemic index than wheat tortillas, helping to control glucose spikes.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese often contains added salt, so people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt varieties.

items.title: Phytates in beans
items.content: Beans contain phytates that may reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lower their levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the tortilla briefly in a skillet or microwave, add the beans, sprinkle with shredded cheese, and optionally top with salsa, guacamole, or fresh cilantro. Serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared tortillas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Store beans and cheese separately in the fridge, and freeze for longer preservation.

content.title: About
content.content: Veal Cordon Bleu is a classic French dish consisting of a thinly pounded veal cutlet stuffed with ham and melted cheese, coated in breadcrumbs and fried until golden. It is served hot, often with a sauce and a side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the early 1920s in Switzerland before becoming popular in France.
Traditional cheeses used are Swiss Emmental or Gruyère.
A chicken version, "Chicken Cordon Bleu," is now common in mass‑market cuisine.
The veal should be pounded to about 0.5 cm thickness for tenderness.
In the United States it is frequently served with mushroom sauce or Béarnaise.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Veal and cheese provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Veal contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, important for bone health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Veal is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The dish is prepared with butter and cheese, making it calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Risk of undercooked meat
items.content: Veal must be fully cooked to prevent food‑borne illnesses.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Ham and cheese are often salty, increasing the dish’s sodium content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Veal Cordon Bleu hot, sliced into portions. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, vegetable ragout, fresh salad, or rice. Mushroom, creamy, mustard, or classic Béarnaise sauces enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and aluminum foil; keep up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Venison is lean meat from a deer, typically taken from the loin or other premium cuts. A venison steak is known for its tender texture, slightly sweet aroma, and low fat content compared with beef. It is commonly grilled, pan‑seared, or roasted and served with sauces and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is one of the most diet‑friendly meats, providing about 120 kcal per 100 g.
The meat is rich in heme iron, making it an excellent source of readily absorbable iron.
In the wild, deer feed on grasses, leaves, and berries, which influence the subtle flavor of their meat.
Venison has a long culinary tradition in Scandinavia, Russia, and North America.
Dry‑aging venison steaks can enhance tenderness and develop deeper flavor notes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Venison contains less saturated fat than beef, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 22 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The iron in venison is highly bioavailable, helping to prevent anemia.

items.title: Source of zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Venison supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to venison, manifested as skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked venison can harbor parasites; thorough cooking is recommended.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Venison is rich in purines, which may be problematic for people with gout or uric acid metabolism disorders.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Venison steak is best cooked quickly over high heat—grill, broiler, or hot pan—to retain juiciness. Marinating in olive oil with rosemary, garlic, and black pepper enhances flavor. Serve with butter‑based sauces, berry chutney, or a vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh venison refrigerated at 0‑2 °C in a sealed bag for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C; it retains quality for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator rather than at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Wasabi peas are roasted green peas coated with a spicy blend of wasabi powder, salt, and sometimes soy sauce. They have a crunchy texture, bright green color, and a distinctive hot‑sharp flavor reminiscent of Japanese wasabi.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The peas used are typically sweet green peas, not the larger field peas.
Commercial wasabi seasoning is often made from horseradish because true wasabi (Wasabia japonica) is expensive and rare.
Wasabi peas are popular as a snack in Asian markets, convenience stores, and movie theaters.
Low‑sodium versions are available because the standard seasoning can be quite salty.
The crunchy peas retain most of the protein and fiber of the original legume.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas contain about 20 % protein, making wasabi peas a good source of plant‑based protein for a snack.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many nut‑based snacks, wasabi peas are low in fat, resulting in fewer calories per serving.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas provide thiamine (B1) and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of wasabi
items.content: Isothiocyanates such as piperine in wasabi have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salty versions can contain up to 400 mg of sodium per 30 g serving, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: People allergic to legumes (peas, beans) may react to wasabi peas.

items.title: Spicy seasoning
items.content: Excessive consumption can irritate the stomach in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Glutamate content
items.content: Some brands add soy sauce, which contains monosodium glutamate that can affect those with sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wasabi peas are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, tossed into salads, rice bowls, or used as a crunchy topping for soups and Asian dishes. They also pair well with dried fruit for a sweet‑spicy mix.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to preserve crunch and flavor. Discard if they develop a stale or rancid smell or lose their crispness.
